To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the dyads undergo rapid photoinduced charge separation in the 0.5–3 ps time range and that the efficiency of charge separation is dependent on the nature of the bridge and the position of attachment of the fullerene to the bacteriochlorin ring.

the dyads undergo rapid (subpicosecond to picoseconds) charge separation, with the rate of charge separation being strongly dependent on the bridge length and the position of attachment of the fullerene to the chlorin.

we synthesized four novel dyads with a bacteriochlorin-fullerene C60 moiety linked at various positions by various bridges, and that we characterized the photophysical and photochemistry properties of these dyads.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new molecular materials with potential for applications in photovoltaics.
the development of novel synthetic strategies for the construction of light-harvestsing antenna/electron-transfer systems based on the bacterio-chlorins and the fullerenes.
the design of new light-harvestant/electron-transfer devices for solar energy conversion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dyads are excellent models for studying charge separation in the light-harvestant/electron-transfer device.
the dyad 1a, which is characterized by a very fast electron transfer (k > 10(10) s(-1)), is the most promising candidate for a light-harvestant/electron-transfer device.
the electron transfer in the dyads is very rapid, but that it is also very sensitive to small structural changes in the dyads.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the dyad with the fullerene attached to the meso-carbon (dyad 2) has the fastest charge separation, followed by the dyad with fullerene attached to an alpha-carbon (dyads 1 and 3) and finally the dyad with a beta-carbon attachment (dyad 4).
the fullerene C60 can be attached to the bacteriochlorin ring by various bridges and at different positions and the electron transfer rate is in the order of 1-10 ps.
the dyads are excellent models for the development of novel antenna/electron-transfer light-harvesters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dyads are able to undergo rapid charge separation and charge recombination, but that the charge recombination rates are strongly influenced by the nature and position of the linker.
the fullerene C60 can be coupled to bacteriochlorin via a wide variety of bridges and positions without significantly affecting the charge-separation dynamics.
the electron transfer rate in all four systems is faster than the rate of singlet excited state quenching by the fullerene acceptor.
